text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin attacked the conservative government's privatisation policy in the run-up to parliamentary elections on Wednesday, saying recent sell-offs had been an "admission of failure."
He accused Prime Minister Alain Juppe's government of using state sales simply to plug a hole in public finances and called for a better balance between markets and the state.

"I find it strange and revealing of an incapacity to manage that this government needs to privatise very large public companies, including some which are jewels of our industry," he said on TF1 French television.
"They need to privatise companies only to balance their budget. It's an admission of failure," he said.
Campaigning for the two-round election on May 25 and June 1, the Socialist party has vowed to halt privatisations.

It has particularly said it would keep 100 percent of France Telecom, in which the government plans to sell a 30-35 percent stake, though Jospin appeared to soften the stance this week by telling a newspaper he would consult staff first.
Education, health, post and transport are other areas which must be guaranteed to the people, the party's programme says.

Jospin acknowledged in Thursday's interview that there was a case for a "certain balance" between private initiative and the kind of public investment which had given France prestige projects including a high-speed railway.
"But I think that if we we want to privatise without thinking about it, if we just want to resort to the market, we would not make progress given the traditions we have," he said.

In an interview to be published on Thursday in business daily Les Echos, Juppe announced plans for a fresh batch of privatisations, possibly including national airline Air France and bank Credit Lyonnais this year, to be followed by insurance group Gan and its banking arm CIC.
The sale of aircraft-maker Aerospatiale-Dassault and defence electronics group Thomson-CSF is already underway.
The government had previously said it did not plan to sell Credit Lyonnais until late 1998 or early 1999. The bank has staged a recovery after suffering losses between 1992 and 1994.
